title_zh: 格伦·贝克（ Glenn Beck ）警告“严肃时代” ，因为非营利组织旨在帮助受迫害的尼日利亚基督徒
author: Jon Brown

title: CNN says a ‘tsunami’ of church closings is coming. The data says otherwise
summary: A recent CNN article warned that a “tsunami” of church closings is poised to remake America. But the numbers tell a quieter story. Closures barely outpace openings, and the most alarming figure counts sold buildings, not dying congregations.
summary_zh: 美国有线电视新闻网（ CNN ）最近的一篇文章警告说，教堂关闭的“海啸”将重塑美国。但这些数字讲述了一个更安静的故事。关闭的速度几乎超过了开口，最令人担忧的数字是出售的建筑物，而不是垂死的会众。
title_zh: 美国有线电视新闻网（ CNN ）表示，教堂关闭的“海啸”即将来临。数据显示并非如此
author: John Stonestreet and Timothy D Padgett

title: Christians with PTSD: Why fear doesn’t mean weak faith
summary: For six years, a deacon took back roads to avoid the interstate where a truck hit him. He believed his fear meant he didn’t trust God enough. Clinical psychologist David Zuccolotto explains why that belief is wrong and what finally helped him drive again.
summary_zh: 六年来，一名执事为了避开一辆卡车撞到他的州际公路，抢回了公路。他认为他的恐惧意味着他不够信任上帝。临床心理学家David Zuccolotto解释了为什么这种信念是错误的，以及最终帮助他再次开车的原因。
title_zh: 患有创伤后应激障碍的基督徒：为什么恐惧并不意味着信仰软弱
author: David Zuccolotto

title: Must Christians vote Democrat? A response to a reader

title_zh: 你的教会可能知道的圣经比你想象的要少（以及该怎么做）
content: In November 1900, Mark Twain delivered a speech titled “The Disappearance of Literature” to the students at Connecticut Wesleyan University. With signature slyness, he told them , “I don’t believe any of you have ever read Paradise Lost , and you don’t want to. That’s something that you just want to take on trust. It’s . . . the definition of a classic—something that everybody wants to have read and nobody wants to read.” Twain was noting the beginning of the illiteracy rockslide that we now witness as an avalanche. The statistics we see in the age of smartphones and social media bear out our eroded literacy: In 2003, average Americans older than age 15 read 21.9 minutes on a given day. By 2010, the number had dropped to 18.3 minutes, and in 2025, it had sunk to 16.2 minutes a day. Imagine how ChatGPT will gut that number even further in the next few years. America is moving rapidly into a postliterate reality, a sort of new Dark Ages, one in which we consume information in images and sound bites, all predigested for us by others. Consider the implications for a system of belief whose transmission from one generation to the next is staked on a book. Christian Literacy Crisis A new survey from Lifeway Research throws into stark relief the chasm between Christian commitment to and knowledge of the Bible. More than 2,000 Christians who attend church in a typical month were surveyed across eight categories of Bible knowledge: major people, passages, events, divisions of Scripture, and more. The researchers designed questions around what would be typically well known rather than obscure. Two out of three respondents scored less than 60, a failing grade. Fifty-five percent could not correctly name the first king of Israel. Only 11 percent could correctly order four major Old Testament events, and only 27 percent could correctly order four major New Testament events. Forty-four percent failed to identify the book of Mark as belonging to the Gospels. Two out of three respondents wrongly believed Hezekiah was a book of the Bible, and 44 percent believed the Gospel of Thomas was as well. Christians have succumbed to the general literacy crisis of the culture. The “people of the Book” don’t read it. The Bible itself, the classic of all classics, has apparently become a book that every Christian wants to have read, and few Christians want to read. If we do read to sustain our faith, we’re more likely to read books about the Bible than the Bible itself. We may consume sermons or podcasts or use devotional resources that cherry-pick verses to give us a positive emotion in 10 minutes or less, but largely, we’ve become curators of other people’s opinions about a book we don’t read ourselves. Failure of Discipleship I believe these results show a failure of discipleship strategies, one with massive implications: We cannot pass along to someone else what we ourselves don’t know. How can the church fulfill the Great Commission if it’s incapable of teaching others to observe everything Jesus commanded? The numbers show we haven’t taught even the basics. If the church were a local public school responsible for teaching basic math and reading, we would receive a failing grade and face funding sanctions. The ‘people of the Book’ don’t read it. Yet, according to a 2024 Lifeway Research survey of 2,620 Protestant pastors, 52 percent are satisfied with the state of discipleship and spiritual formation in their churches. Twenty-nine percent report that they regularly evaluate discipleship progress among their congregations. When asked their first priority in discipleship, the largest number responded that it be “biblical knowledge focused.” And in response to the question “What approaches does your church specifically use to disciple and encourage the spiritual development of adults in your congregation?” 89 percent responded the sermon, the top answer by a 20-point gap, with adult Sunday school listed second. The sermon matters enormously. But we’re learning that the sermon alone cannot do the heavy lifting of solving the Bible literacy crisis. It’s a passive learning environment, a one-way communication. Imagine if your local public school believed passively listening to a lecture was the only way to form students into contributing citizens. Why does the local church think people comprehensively learn the Bible in such settings? Imagine also if your local public school recommended peer-led discussion groups as a primary vehicle for educating students. Imagine if the time spent in these groups was used to reflect for 30 minutes or so on what was taught in a lecture several days before: Mrs. Harker lectures on the quadratic equation for 30 minutes on Monday; students discuss how to apply the quadratic equation to their lives for 30 minutes on Wednesday. Who’s passing an algebra exam? Yet, 95 percent of pastors surveyed responded that discipleship isn’t completed in a program but in a relationship. Hence, the ubiquity of the community-group model in evangelical churches. We Know What to Do The wildest part of this disconnect about how to teach what’s good in a way that sticks is that we know the answer. The answer isn’t a new thing but an old thing recently forgotten. The church must return to its roots as the solver of illiteracy, both within its walls and also without. Education pastors can be tempted to dabble, trying one thing or another to see what their church members might find interesting, buying the latest study from a Christian publisher on the assumption it’s good. The idea that there are well-attested best practices for Christian education seems to have gotten lost. Just like a healthy local school, churches need to reclaim active, dedicated learning environments—spaces designated explicitly for the purpose of teaching the Bible. They need to think like educators: What is the scope and sequence for what we’ll teach? And they need to ask a better question than “What do my congregants want to learn?” I didn’t want to learn grammar, but thank goodness, Mrs. Wagner knew I needed it and taught it to me anyway. Her evident enthusiasm for the topic fascinated me. What was I missing that she knew? I learned grammar in a dialogic space taught by a subject-matter expert with an evident love for her subject. That love was contagious. Imagine if the church taught people the Bible like Mrs. Wagner taught grammar. It might become the classic of classics that every Christian actually wants to read. Christians possess the most beautiful and compelling book of all. Because a book forms the foundation of our faith, Christians have always been invested in solving illiteracy. We’ve striven to train people to read because reading is essential to the promulgation of our faith. The roots of public education and university systems lie in Christian efforts to grow literacy. The availability of vernacular translations of the Bible is the result of a concern for readability for all. Sunday school began in the late 1700s as an effort to educate children who worked in factories prior to child labor laws, seizing their one day off work as a literacy opportunity. Christians have been literacy champions in previous dark ages—and Christians can be again. Don’t Look Away In the first article I ever wrote for The Gospel Coalition back in 2012, I considered the Bible literacy crisis: “Why does biblical ignorance continue to dog the church, despite the good intentions of leadership to obey the Great Command to make disciples? I believe the answer lies in our definition of a disciple. A disciple is, literally, a learner—one who follows another’s teaching.” Fourteen years later, I’m still asking church leaders to remember to teach learners as the most basic function of discipleship, and to do so with proven tools. Don’t look away from the problem. Don’t tell yourself it’s the problem of the church down the road. In a cultural literacy freefall, all churches will feel the negative effects in Bible liter

1900年11月,马克·吐温向康涅狄格韦斯利安大学的学生发表了题为“文学失踪”的演讲。 他对他们说:「我不相信你们谁读过失乐园, 这是你想要信任的东西。 这是.
一个经典的定义——人人都想读,没有人想读。” Twain注意到文盲的起步, 我们在智能手机和社交媒体时代所看到的统计数据证明了我们被侵蚀的识字率: 2003年,15岁以上的美国人平均每天读取21.9分。
至2010年已降至18.3分,2025年已下沉至每天16.2分. 想象一下ChatGPT在未来几年里会如何进一步切断这个数字. 美国正在迅速进入一个后文化的现实, 一种新的黑暗时代, 在其中,我们消耗信息 在图像和声音叮咬, 这一切都被其他人预想。
考虑一下对一种信仰体系的影响,这种信仰体系的代代相传被放在一本书上。 基督教识字危机 生活之路研究的一项新调查使基督教对《圣经》的承诺和对《圣经》的了解之间的裂痕大为缓解。
在典型的一个月内参加教堂的基督徒有2000多人接受过8个类别的圣经知识调查:主要人物、经文、活动、圣经的分化等等。 研究人员围绕什么是通常众所周知的而不是模糊的问题。 3个受访者中有2个得分不足60分,成绩不及格.
百分之五十五无法正确命名以色列第一任国王. 只有11%的人可以正确订购四起"旧约"重大事件,只有27%的人可以正确订购四起"新约"重大事件. 百分之四十四未能将"马克"一书认定为属于"福音".
三分之二的受访者错误地认为"赫泽基亚"是"圣经"一书,44%的人认为"托马斯福音"也是". 基督教徒已经屈服于文化的普遍识字危机. " 书生"不读. 圣经本身,是所有经典的经典,显然已经成为了每个基督徒都想阅读的一本书,很少有基督徒想阅读.
如果我们真的读到来维持我们的信仰,我们更可能阅读有关圣经的书籍,而不是圣经本身. 我们可能会使用布道或播客, 或利用奉献资源, 挑出诗句,
散会失败 我认为这些结果表明门徒战略失败, 我们不能把自己所不知道的东西传给别人。 如果教会不能教别人观察耶稣的旨意, 数字显示我们甚至没有教授基本知识。
如果教堂是一所负责教授基本数学和阅读的当地公立学校,我们就会得到一个不及格的分数,并面临资金制裁. " 书中的人 " 不读。 然而,根据2024年对2,620名新教牧师进行的生活道研究调查,52%的人对其教会的门徒身份和精神形成状况感到满意.
29%的人报告说,他们定期评估其教会中的门徒进步。
当被问及他们在门徒中的首要地位时,人数最多的回答是“圣经知识集中”。 在回答“你的教堂对门徒具体使用什么方法,鼓励成年人在会堂中的精神发展?” 的问题时,89%的人回答布道,即最高的回答是20分的差距,成人星期日学校排在第二位。
讲道很重要 但我们知道,单凭布道并不能解决圣经的通晓危机。 这是被动的学习环境, 想象一下,如果当地的公立学校 相信被动地听一个演讲 是培养学生 贡献公民的唯一途径。
当地教会为何认为人们在这样的环境下全面学习"圣经"? 也想一想,如果你的地方公立学校建议由同行领导的讨论小组作为教育学生的主要工具。 想象一下,如果在这些团体中度过的时间被用来反思几天前在一次讲座中所教的内容:
哈克周一关于四分法方程式的讲座为30分钟;学生周三讨论如何将四分法方程式应用于他们的生活30分钟. 谁要通过代数考试? 但95%的受访牧师回应说, 门徒身份不是在一个计划中完成, 因此,福音教会中普遍存在社区团体模式。
我们知道该做什么 最疯狂的部分 如何教导什么是好 的方式坚持, 答案并不是新事物, 教堂必须恢复其根基,作为解决文盲问题的手段,无论是在其墙上还是在墙外。
教育牧师可能会被诱惑去玩弄, 尝试看他们教会成员会发现什么有趣的东西, 基督教教育方面有经过充分检验的最佳做法的想法似乎已经消失。
与健康的当地学校一样,教会需要恢复积极、专注的学习环境——明确指定用于教授圣经的空间。 他们需要像教育家一样思考: 我们将要教授的内容的范围和顺序是什么? 他们需要问一个比“我的教友们想学什么”更好的问题。 我不想学语法,但谢天谢地,夫人。
瓦格纳知道我需要它 并且教给我 她对这个话题的明显热情让我着迷. 我错过了什么 她知道? 我在一个对话空间学习了语法, 由一位主题专家教授, 爱是传染性的。 想象一下如果教会教人们像瓦格纳夫人那样教授了文法的圣经.
这可能会成为每个基督徒真正想阅读的经典. 基督徒拥有最美丽和最有说服力的书 因为一本书构成了我们信仰的基础,所以基督徒总是被投入解决文盲问题. 我们努力训练人们阅读,
公共教育和大学制度的根源在于基督教努力提高识字率。 圣经的方言翻译的可用性是关注全民可读性的结果. 星期天学校于1700年代后期开始,以努力教育那些在童工法之前在工厂工作的儿童,抓住他们一天的休息时间作为识字的机会.
基督徒在之前的黑暗时代是识字的冠军——基督徒也可以再次成为. 别走开 我在2012年为"福音联盟"撰写的第一篇文章中,认为"圣经的通晓危机":"圣经的无知为什么继续支持教会,尽管领导者有服从"大命令"让门徒成为门徒的良好意图?
我相信答案就在于我们对门徒的定义 从字面上讲,一个弟子是一个学习者——一个听从他人教导的人。 十四年后, 我仍要求教会领袖们记住, 也不要忽略问题。 别告诉自己,
在文化知识自由落地中,所有教会都会在"圣经"一升中感受到负面影响

title: Does Christianity Make Sense? On God, Evil, and the Ache (with Gavin Ortlund)
summary: Gavin Ortlund joins Collin Hansen to discuss apologetics and why Christianity makes sense.
summary_zh: 不久前,我儿子问我 大卫国王在塞缪尔8号杀死的所有人 我们一直读这本书, 他有权被打扰。 我们曾讨论过为什么他不紧张,我们如何发展道德本能,以及我们如何回应因旧约中这些和类似说法而拒绝上帝的人。 我们一起做杂技表演 我将指向我的朋友Gavin Ortlund的YouTube频道, 然后,几年后,我将指给他看加文的著作,包括他的最新著作《基督教为何要讲道理:关于耶稣的一书、世界的谜题以及你心中的长寿》(Zondervan Reflectionive ) 。
title_zh: 基督教有意义吗？论上帝、邪恶和痛苦（与Gavin Ortlund合作）
content: Not long ago, my son asked me about all the people King David killed in 2 Samuel 8. We’ve been reading through that book during family devotions before bed. He’s right to be disturbed. So we had a conversation about why he’s unnerved, how we develop moral instincts, and how we’d respond to someone who rejects God because of these and similar accounts in the Old Testament. We did apologetics together. As he gets a little older, I’ll point him toward the YouTube channel of my friend Gavin Ortlund, who does an excellent job of answering many hard questions about Christianity and the Bible. Then, a few years later, I’ll point him to Gavin’s books, including his latest, Why Christianity Makes Sense: A Book About Jesus, the Mysteries of the World, and the Longings in Your Heart (Zondervan Reflective). He’s back on Gospelbound to discuss all things apologetics, from the multiverse, to slavery, to morality as merely a taste for sugar, to winning the lottery 10 billion times in a row. In This Episode 00:00 – Why people may be more open to spiritual answers today 03:36 – “The ache” and the longing for transcendence 09:29 – What about Christianity makes the least sense to Gavin? 11:39 – The problem of evil and the limits of tidy answers 19:09 – The growing challenge of divine hiddenness 24:34 – Fine-tuning and the odds of a life-permitting universe 32:07 – Is morality without God just a matter of taste? 37:25 – Slavery, the Bible, and the Christian roots of human equality 42:23 – Why fulfilled prophecy surprised Gavin 48:00 – What apologetic questions should Christians prepare for next? Resources Mentioned: Why Christianity Makes Sense by Gavin Ortlund Mere Christianity by C. S. Lewis Making Sense of God by Timothy Keller The Reason for God by Timothy Keller The Brothers Karamazov by Fyodor Dostoevsky Bullies and Saints by John Dickson Dominion by Tom Holland Gavin Ortlund’s YouTube channel, “ Truth Unites “ The Keller Center for Cultural Apologetics SIGN UP for my newsletter, Unseen Things . title: I Was a Justice Warrior. I Needed the Whole Gospel. You Do Too.
summary: Most Christians today see these two gospel aspects as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined.
summary_zh: 从2016年到2018年,我是一个社交媒体正义战士. 我花时间在Facebook和Twitter上, 如果你读到我的文章,你可能没有猜到我在郊区一个保守的基督教家庭长大,或者我从4岁开始每天在基督教学校接受教育。 在我成长的过程中,我学会了基督教信仰的丰富深度.
title_zh: 我是一名正义战士。我需要完整的福音。你也是。
content: From 2016 to 2018, I was a social media justice warrior. I spent my time on Facebook and Twitter confronting the powerful and comfortable, championing justice issues, and fighting for racial and political reconciliation. If you read my posts, you might not have guessed that I grew up in a conservative Christian home nestled in suburbia, or that I spent every day of my education, starting at age 4, in Christian schools. In my upbringing, I learned the rich depths of the Christian faith. I surrendered my life to Jesus, and I learned that Jesus came to seek to save the lost. Yet that evangelistically oriented world of my youth was intentionally sanitized and separated from the painful realities of poverty and injustice just 10 minutes down the road. When I discovered this disparity, I became a justice warrior online. And while that posture was certainly a reaction to my upbringing, I wasn’t being a hypocrite. My social media advocacy reflected my actual life. I’ve lived and worked in an underresourced neighborhood since 2001. During my first 15 years in the neighborhood, I grew burdened over the disconnect I saw between the conditions my neighbors faced daily and how many in the American church live. The political, racial, and socioeconomic divide between my church life and neighborhood gutted me. So when I went online, I was convinced I was sharing the true gospel. Yet that “gospel” I shared was merely centered on producing tangible results in the here and now, not on affecting eternity. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. Two Gospel Aspects I began to see two aspects in the biblical gospel. Let’s call them the gospel of the cross and the gospel of the kingdom . The gospel of the cross is the good news that Jesus Christ saves and adopts believers as his children through his substitutionary death and glorious resurrection. We’re all born alienated from God. In sin, we’re his enemies. In Christ, as we believe the good news, we’re reconciled to God (Rom. 5:6–10) and assured of eternal life with him (John 3:16). As Peter writes, “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Pet. 3:18). Moreover, the cross aspect of the gospel emphasizes that those entrusted with this message must share it with a lost and dying world (Matt. 28:18–20). The gospel of the cross must be heralded; it must be proclaimed. It is the priority. From this gospel flows every good gift. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. The gospel of the kingdom is the good news that God’s will for justice, goodness, and peace is already being unleashed. As God’s children, believers are invited to play a part in seeing that kingdom mission come to fruition. Jesus begins his ministry by preaching a message that proclaims “good news to the poor” and “liberty to the . . . oppressed” (Luke 4:18). He calls his hearers to repent, including from ways they’ve oppressed and neglected the poor (Matt. 3:2; 4:17). He specifically rebukes the Pharisees for neglecting “the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (23:23). Paul, too, teaches that the gospel not only reunites us to God but also works justice by reconciling divided peoples to one another in the church. He writes, “For [Christ] himself is our peace, who has made us both [ethnic groups] one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Eph. 2:14). We fulfill the law and live out the gospel’s kingdom implications through our identity as shalom -makers (Matt. 5:9). The kingdom aspect of the gospel equips us with a vision for pursuing God’s will “on earth as it is in heaven” (6:10), that is, for seeing all things made new (Rev. 21:5). This gospel of the kingdom must be lived out through embodied action. Mapping Our Approaches to Cross and Kingdom Most Christians today rightly see these two gospel aspects—the message proper and its kingdom implications—as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined. As a result, many emphasize only one aspect or the other. And sadly, some neglect both these aspects of the gospel altogether. Nicholas Wolterstorff writes that shalom is “a harmony and delight in all of one’s relationships: between us and God, us and other people, us and other cultures, us and creation, and between us and our very selves.” In the four-quadrant grid below, I’ve mapped out the ways we typically approach the cross and kingdom aspects of the gospel. (For more, see section II.3 of The Gospel Coalition’s Theological Vision for Ministry .) Christ’s sacrifice on the cross restores us to harmony and delight with God. This is our most important relationship, and it’s represented on the diagram by the upward-pointing vertical axis. A kingdom emphasis on harmony and delight in other people, other cultures, and the creation is represented by the rightward-pointing horizontal axis. Quadrants II and IV represent two errors—the false choice of emphasizing either the cross or kingdom while neglecting the other. Many American Christians have been ensnared by one of these two quadrants. Quadrant III designates a total neglect of both cross and also kingdom. All these disconnects result from misunderstanding who a Christian is and what a Christian should do in this broken world. Quadrant IV: Individualized Gospel Advocates of an individualized gospel (quadrant IV) want to get people saved for the afterlife without stressing the social implications for this life. When sinners are saved, we always celebrate! However, Christians who fit in this quadrant often don’t emphasize the kingdom aspect of the gospel. Such individuals and churches may financially support ministries in underresourced neighborhoods but don’t often emphasize transformative service there. Many such churches and their members may not understand or appreciate the depth and range of problems in struggling communities, even in neighborhoods not far from them. Quadrant II: Social Gospel Advocates of the social gospel seek to meet people’s imminent needs but neglect their ultimate need of the salvation Jesus offers. This is a scandalous compromise, and it’s the false gospel I believed for nearly a decade and then proclaimed as a social media justice warrior. My wife and I moved into our underresourced neighborhood to live close to the school where I served for 18 years. Living and working among the poor showed me that many people need more than hearing about Jesus alone. They needed tangible help. Many of my quadrant IV friends concluded my neighbors were ignorant, dangerous, and to be avoided. So I reacted to my peers by propelling myself into the social gospel. Most Christians today see these two gospel aspects as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined. The social gospel is an late 19th- and early 20th-century theological movement focused on breaking the chains of oppression and championing the poor. Advocates seek to make Christ’s kingdom manifest on earth through acts of charity, philanthropy, and just legislation. Some social-gospel advocates choose to live close to the poor to improve their neighborhoods and lives. Yet the social gospel focuses solely on meeting imminent needs. It neglects preaching Christ as the sinner’s Savior. In fact, many social-gospel advocates reject the evangelical gospel and biblical authority. 尼古拉斯·沃尔特斯托夫(Nicholas Wolterstorff)写道:"在一个人的所有关系中,我们与上帝、我们与其他人、我们与其他文化、我们与创造之间,以及我们与我们自身之间,都是和谐和愉快的"。 在下面的四平地网格中, 我绘制了我们一般处理福音的十字和王国方面的方式。

一个王国在其他人,其他文化中强调和谐与快乐,而创造者则以右向的横向轴为代表. 四方二和四代表两个错误——错误的选择是强调十字或王国,而忽略另一个。 许多美国基督徒被这两个四重奏之一所迷惑.

然而,社会福音完全侧重于满足紧迫的需要。 它忽略了宣扬基督是罪人救世主. 事实上,许多社会-神道倡导者拒绝福音和圣经权威. 许多为资源不足的社区服务的教会组织被社会神学所牵制.

title: Lessons from Lloyd-Jones on Preaching and Politics
summary: Here are three lessons we can learn from Martyn Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis.
summary_zh: “我从未担心过像希特勒这样的人。 ” 这不是一个疯子或有权免于战争恐怖的人的说法。 这些是一位牧师的话,他受到纳粹领导人的直接威胁,他穿上了神的全盔并准备出战。 阿道夫·希特勒于1939年9月1日入侵波兰;
title_zh: 劳埃德-琼斯关于讲道和政治的教训
content: “I was never worried for a second about a man like Hitler.” This isn’t the statement of a madman or of someone privileged enough to be removed from the horrors of the war. These are the words of a pastor who was under immediate threat from the Nazi leader and who’d put on the full armor of God and prepared for battle. Adolf Hitler invaded Poland on September 1, 1939; the very next day, Martyn Lloyd-Jones was installed as an associate pastor at Westminster Chapel in London, where he would faithfully preach for the next 30 years. One year after the preacher took the pulpit, Hitler began his bombing campaign over London. Of the roughly 700 churches in the area, 624 were damaged by the bombings and 91 were totally destroyed. To the surprise of many, Westminster Chapel, one of London’s largest churches at the time, wasn’t destroyed in the bombing blitz. Iain Murray, in his classic biography on Lloyd-Jones , writes about one Sunday morning when a bomb hit close to the Chapel right in the middle of Lloyd-Jones’s Lord’s Day prayer. The bomb shook the entire building, and plaster and dust fell down on the congregation, including on “the Doctor,” as Lloyd-Jones was known. After a pause, Lloyd-Jones simply continued his prayer and the service went forward unimpeded. Lloyd-Jones offers a needed corrective to our politically anxious times. Some Christians resort to despair, while others attempt revolution. What we need is a political theology that still preaches Christ when the bombs go off. Here are three lessons we can learn from Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis. Refuse Saul’s Armour When it became apparent that England was entering the war, Lloyd-Jones sent his wife and their two children back to Wales and away from the city, not knowing what would become of it. In a brief and urgent correspondence to his wife, he writes , “Leave yourself and me too, and everything in God’s hand and you will find peace and rest.” With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. Because of fear and panic, many began to abandon the weapons of the church and replace them with the weapons of the state. But Lloyd-Jones refused to blur the lines. When the war was at its worst and his congregation had been reduced to few because of death and displacement, he remained resolute in affirming 2 Corinthians 10:4: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (KJV). Lloyd-Jones refused to allow revolutionary alliances and tactics to infiltrate the church: Alas, far too often the church has tried to meet the world and its persecuting power with like weapons to those employed by the enemy. She has made alliances with the state and she has tried to strengthen herself in a material sense. She has been slow to discover what David discovered long ago in his fight with Goliath, that she cannot fight in the armour of Saul, but must ever use her own weapons with which she is familiar and with which she is meant to use. Lloyd-Jones saw a parallel between those in Saul’s armory who were looking to outfit David for battle with new calls from within the church to align herself with the state. Like David’s pitiful sling, prayer may appear in the world’s eyes woefully insufficient weaponry against fascism. But God’s weapons are greater than the weapons of men. Reject the Partisan Gospel Lloyd-Jones saw that the church was particularly vulnerable to political idolatry when fear had gripped the people. Like the Israelites shaking at the sight of Goliath, we often feel the only reasonable response is to find our own “strong man” to fight our battles. Throughout the church’s history, we’ve often turned to national politics. In a talk titled “ Living in Revolutionary Times ,” Lloyd-Jones rebukes the evangelicals of his day, who “seem to think that they are innovators in saying that we should all be taking an interest in politics and social matters.” But this is nothing new. Lloyd-Jones recalls, “They do not seem to have heard of the ‘social gospel’ craze of the earlier part of this century. All this has been tried with great thoroughness.” A preacher unaware of the dangerous pitfalls the church has already fallen into is sure to lead his congregation into one of those pits. This was the great danger, in Lloyd-Jones’s mind, of harnessing power for the church through political means. Any talk of political revolution inside the church—or a call to Christianize the nation—is a call to put on Saul’s armor again. In that same talk, Lloyd-Jones cautions preachers against the temptation to quickly gather a crowd by preaching politics. His words feel even more timely today: I well remember certain men who were concerned about social and political matters, and who constantly preached on such themes, and packed their chapels for a while, but only as long as they preached politics. The moment they began to preach the gospel truly the crowds left them. Politically-minded people are always ready to make use of the church, but they always abandon and shun her when she ceases to be of any value to them. American pulpits have been infected with this kind of partisan preaching for decades now, on both the left and right. It draws crowds but does a disservice to the gospel. It’s important for Christians to offer a robust political and social ethic, but not at the expense of the gospel. The former flows from the latter, and the order is irreversible. Remember the ‘Leaven’ For Lloyd-Jones, spiritual resurrection—not political revolution—would save the world. The church didn’t need a theology of liberation but a theology of “leaven.” Drawing a straight line through the New Testament, he says , “The Christian is represented as ‘salt’ in society and ‘leaven,’ and surely the whole point of those comparisons is that Christian influence is to be a quiet influence and a slow process of influencing society.” Any talk of political revolution inside the church—or a call to Christianize the nation—is a call to put on Saul’s armor again. In times of political crisis, such as our own, we’re tempted to forget this basic biblical principle. We must remember that “the kingdom of God is like leaven” (Matt. 13:33). If we’re to have social and political influence, it’ll only happen through preaching and preserving the gospel, so that regenerate Christians can be salt and light in the public square. On May 21, 1943, when Westminster Chapel was finally seeing signs of stability after the bombings, Lloyd-Jones wrote a letter responding to a congregant who was thanking him for his faithful preaching. He ended by saying , “The supreme need of the hour is intense prayer for spiritual revival on the part of Christian people.” The Doctor was interested in treating the disease, not the symptoms. That’s why he could speak with such audacity, testifying that he was “never worried for a second about a man like Hitler.” As wicked as Hitler was, he was merely symptomatic of the spiritual disease of the human heart—to which the gospel alone is the cure.

“我从未担心过像希特勒这样的人。” 这不是一个疯子或有权免于战争恐怖的人的说法。 这些是一位牧师的话,他受到纳粹领导人的直接威胁,他穿上了神的全盔并准备出战。 阿道夫·希特勒于1939年9月1日入侵波兰;
第二天,马丁·劳埃德-琼斯 在伦敦的威斯敏斯特礼拜堂 担任助理牧师 他将在接下来的30年里 忠实地传教 传教士取道后一年,希特勒开始对伦敦的轰炸战役. 在该地区大约700所教堂中,有624所被炸毁,91所被完全摧毁。
令许多威斯敏斯特礼拜堂(Westminster Chapel)惊讶的是, Iain Murray在他的关于劳埃德-琼斯的经典传记中写道,
炸弹震动了整个建筑,石膏和灰尘落在会众上,包括劳埃德-琼斯所闻的“医生”上。 在暂停后,劳埃德-琼斯只是继续了他的祈祷,礼拜无阻地向前. Lloyd -Jones为我们的政治焦虑时期提供了必要的纠正。 一些基督徒诉诸于绝望,而另一些人则试图革命.
我们需要的是政治神学,当炸弹爆炸时,它仍然宣扬基督。 在政治危机时期, 我们可以从劳埃德-琼斯的部里学到三个教训。 当英格兰显然正在进入战争时,劳埃德-琼斯将他的妻子和他们的两个孩子送回威尔士并远离了这座城市,却不知道会发生什么事。
在一封与他妻子的简短而紧急的信件中,他写道:"也离开你和我,以及上帝手中的一切,你会得到平和与安息". 随着炸弹高空飞来,教堂里许多人呼吁革命,但劳埃德-琼斯呼吁祈祷. 随着炸弹高空飞来,教堂里许多人呼吁革命,但劳埃德-琼斯呼吁祈祷.
由于恐惧和恐慌,许多人开始放弃教会的武器,取而代之的是国家的武器. 但劳埃德-琼斯拒绝模糊界限.
当战争处于最坏的状态,由于死亡和流离失所,他的会众减少到很少的时候,他仍然坚决申明2个科林斯人10:4:“我们的战争武器不是同性相通的,而是通过上帝而强大的力量来拉倒坚固的阵地”(KJV)。
劳埃德-琼斯拒绝允许革命联盟和战术渗透到教会中去: 唉,教会经常试图用类似武器来对付被敌人所雇佣的人来对付世界及其迫害的力量. 她与国家结盟,并试图在物质意义上加强自己。
她一直缓慢地发现大卫很久以前在与高丽的战斗中发现的东西,即她不能在索尔的盔甲上出战,而必须永远使用她熟悉并打算使用的武器.
劳埃德-琼斯在索尔的军械库里看到类似的情况, 与大卫的悲哀一样,祈祷可能出现在世界的眼中,令人悲哀的是,反对法西斯主义的武器不足。 但上帝的武器比人的武器还多
反对党的福音 劳埃德-琼斯看到,当恐惧笼罩人民时,教会特别容易受到政治偶像崇拜的影响。 像在高丽之光下摇晃的以色列人一样,我们常常感到唯一的合理反应是找到我们自己的“强人”来战斗。 我们经常转向国家政治。
在一篇题为“生活在革命时报”的演讲中,劳埃德-琼斯斥责了当时的福音派,他们“似乎认为他们是创新者,认为我们大家都应该关心政治和社会事务。 但这不是什么新鲜事。 劳埃德-琼斯回忆说, " 他们似乎没有听说过本世纪上半叶的 " 社会福音 " 狂热。
所有这一切都经过了非常彻底的尝试。” 一个牧师不知道教堂已经陷入了危险的陷阱 肯定会把他的会众带到其中的一个坑里 在劳埃德-琼斯的心目中,这是通过政治手段掌握教会权力的巨大危险。
任何关于教会内部政治革命的言论, 在同一话中,劳埃德-琼斯告诫道教士不要通过宣扬政治来迅速聚集一众的诱惑.
他的话今天感觉更加及时:我清楚地记得某些关心社会和政治事务的人,他们不断地宣扬这些主题,打包他们的礼拜堂一段时间,但只要他们宣扬政治. 当他们开始宣扬福音时, 群众真的离开了他们。
有政治思想的人总是准备利用教堂,但当她不再对他们有任何价值时,他们总是抛弃并避开她. 美国的纸币 已经感染这种 党派传道 几十年了,左右两侧。 它吸引了人群,但不利于福音。
基督徒必须提供强有力的政治和社会道德, 前者从后者而来,而顺序是不可逆转的. 记住劳埃德-琼斯的"离开"(Leaven for Lloyd-Jones),精神复活——而不是政治革命——将拯救世界.
教会并不需要解放神学, 在新约中画出一条直线,他说 : “ 基督徒在社会中被代表为`盐'和`离开',这些比较的全部要点无疑是,基督教的影响是一种静默的影响,是影响社会的缓慢过程。 ” 任何关于教会内部政治革命的言论...
或号召基督教化国家, 在政治危机时期,比如我们自己的时代,我们想忘记这个基本的圣经原则。 我们必须记住,“上帝的王国就像一去不复返”(Matt. 13:33)。
我们只有通过传道和维护福音, 才能产生社会和政治影响, 1943年5月21日,当威斯敏斯特礼拜堂终于在轰炸后看到稳定的迹象时,劳埃德-琼斯写了一封信,答复了一位正在感谢他忠实地传道的教友.
他最后说,“最需要的是基督教人民强烈地祈祷精神复兴。” 医生对治疗疾病感兴趣,而不是症状。
因此,他可以如此大胆地说话,证明他“从来不担心像希特勒这样的人。 ” 与希特勒一样邪恶,他只是人类心灵的精神疾病的症状——只有福音才能治愈。
author: Dylan Budd

title: Develop Healthy Tech Habits with Your Teen
summary: ‘Scroll Less, Live More’ helps teens and parents develop the tech skills they need to live a life rooted in reality and steeped in wisdom.
summary_zh: 每个星期天晚上,在青年团体,我们通过唱歌进行礼拜的时间,接着是简短的布道,然后是小组讨论。 我带领的高中生们都懂规矩 在打开"圣经"前,把椅子拉入一圈. 然后我们拿出我们的电话 把它们堆在地上 戒指中间。 我们不会再碰那些屏幕, 电话堆是一个简单的习惯。
title_zh: 与青少年一起养成健康的科技习惯
content: Each Sunday night at youth group, our time of worship through singing is followed by a short sermon then small-group discussion. The high school kids in the group I lead know the routine. Before we open the Scriptures, we pull our chairs into a circle. Then we take out our phones and stack them in a pile on the floor in the middle of the ring. We won’t touch those screens again until the Bible-study hour is done. The phone stack is a simple habit. But it’s helped the students in our group pay closer attention to both one another and the Bible text. In his practical new book, Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Healthy Tech Habits for Teens , Samuel James commends a number of similar practices. His goal is to give teenagers “a vivid picture of what it looks like to apply [biblical] wisdom to technology usage in today’s digital age” (155). James recognizes that simple, repeatable practices can help young people resist the foolishness today’s tech promotes so they can instead grow in the fear of the Lord. Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More builds on the foundation James laid in his previous book for adults, Digital Liturgies: Rediscovering Christian Wisdom in an Online Age . One of his main premises is that technology isn’t neutral. Rather, it’s a powerful force that “shapes and influences us in ways we aren’t always aware of” (30). One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. To illustrate this truth, James points to tech invented in the 19th century: Before the telephone . . . people just accepted that if they weren’t in the same room as somebody, they couldn’t communicate with that person in the moment. After the telephone was introduced, being able to communicate with someone in a different place at any time became not only possible but also important. (125) Similarly, 21st-century tech such as generative AI brings with it both new possibilities and greater expectations: “AI’s capability to produce an amazing variety of work and art with very little direct human involvement creates an expectation that using it regularly for these purposes is normal” (127). The more we off-load our creativity and effort to it, the more we believe we should do so. One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. Digital technology changes us in other ways too. James draws on the work of tech realists such as Neil Postman , Nicholas Carr , and Marshall McLuhan , but he makes their perspective accessible for adolescents. James repeatedly shows young people how poor digital habits affect their cognition, emotions, and relationships. Living on a phone will slow down thinking, leaving teens feeling anxious, or even angry, amid daily interactions that then become more awkward and strained. Way of Wisdom: Guard Your Heart How do we help young people avoid this path? James gives teens some practical encouragements, telling them to charge their phones somewhere other than in their bedrooms overnight. He also provides a list self-examination questions to help them grow in self-awareness and he appeals to family rules such as only using devices in open areas of the home. But ultimately, James is convinced that using technology well involves more than simply following a list of dos and don’ts. He writes, We don’t need a huge list of rules that will have to be updated every time Apple releases a new phone or a new social media app; we need something that will help us determine how to use technology well in any circumstance. We need wisdom. (16–17) Proverbs says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight” (9:10). James is clear that growing in wisdom and the knowledge of the Lord requires more than adjusting one’s screen-time settings; it takes guarding one’s heart. James encourages teens to think of their hearts as a palace where a king or queen lives. He says, “In any royal palace, you’re sure to find soldiers keeping watch over who and what has access to the very important king or queen inside”; those guards, he contends, are our habits, and “the strength of the soldiers determines how protected the palace is” (158). Early in the book, James calls teens to learn discernment. As he unpacks this habit, he warns them away from the siren song of social media influencers who question parental authority: “When an online influencer who doesn’t know you or care for you speaks about your parents or mentors in a way that makes you want to trust those people less and the influencer more, that’s a massive sign that what you’re listening to is false” (44). Yet James doesn’t merely tell young people to flee digital technology’s dangers; he also beckons them to put on habits that will help them cultivate virtue, in-person friendship, accountability, industrious work, creativity, and rest. For Parents Too Many of these habits are relational. In his introduction, for example, James encourages teens to read his book with a parent, teacher, pastor, or mentor. The discussion questions he includes at the end of each chapter make this counsel practical. This counsel is also wise, because while Scroll Less, Live More is a book for teens, it’s a book for parents too. As a parent and youth worker, I found James’s encouragement to develop a habit of self-awareness convicting. He calls readers to pay attention when being online leads to feelings of anger, anxiety, or boredom so that you know when to “log off and touch grass.” Listless boredom is a form of the sin of acedia : “Spiritual laziness that causes you to fill up on meaningless things so much that you cannot delight in God” (65). He nailed me. How many times do I fill life’s quiet moments—waiting in a line, a few minutes between meetings, or sadly even lulls in conversation—by pulling out my phone instead of being attentive to nature, the people around me, and the Lord? Listless boredom is a form of the sin of acedia . I can get frustrated when I see this tendency in teens, but as Brett McCracken writes , “What parents model with our own devices ultimately matters more than what we say to our kids about them.” James’s book helped me see ways I’ve failed to fight endless scrolling in my own life. As parents, we need God’s Spirit to help us grow in self-awareness about our tech habits. We need his grace to help us confess those failures to the teens we parent and lead. And we need a heart of wisdom and phone-stack intentionality, not just at youth group meetings but throughout our lives. Scroll Less, Live More helps teens and parents develop the tech skills they need to live a life rooted in reality and steeped in wisdom.

每个星期天晚上,在青年团体,我们通过唱歌进行礼拜的时间,接着是简短的布道,然后是小组讨论。 我带领的高中生们都懂规矩 在打开"圣经"前,把椅子拉入一圈. 然后我们拿出我们的电话 把它们堆在地上 戒指中间。
我们不会再碰那些屏幕, 电话堆是一个简单的习惯。 这帮助了我们团体的学生更密切地关注彼此和圣经文本。 在他实用的新书"Scroll Less"(Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Health Tech Habits for Teens)中,塞缪尔·詹姆斯称赞了一些类似的做法.
他的目标是让青少年 " 生动地了解在当今数字时代将[圣经上 智慧应用于技术应用的外表 " (155)。 詹姆斯认识到简单、可重复的做法可以帮助年轻人抵制当今技术推广的愚蠢,让他们在上帝的恐惧中成长。
Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More 在他的前作中为成年人奠定的基础上, 科技并非中立。 而是一股强大的力量, “塑造并影响我们,
技术改变我们的方法之一是改变我们的期望。 为了说明这个事实,詹姆斯指出19世纪发明的技术: 在电话之前, 人们刚刚接受, 如果他们不和别人在同一间屋子里,
在电话引入后,能够随时与另一个地方的某个人通信不仅成为可能,而且非常重要.
(125) 同样地,21世纪的技术,如基因人工智能,也带来了新的可能性和更大的期望: " 人工智能在人类很少直接参与的情况下生产出惊人的作品和艺术的能力,使人们期望经常用于这些目的是正常的 " (127)。 我们越是放弃我们的创造力和努力,我们就越相信我们应该这样做。
技术改变我们的方法之一是改变我们的期望。 数字技术也以其他方式改变我们。 James借鉴了Neil Postman、Nicholas Carr、Marshall McLuhan等科技现实主义者的作品, 詹姆斯反复地向年轻人展示,不良的数字习惯如何影响他们的认知,情感和关系.
生活在电话里会减缓思考, 让青少年感到焦虑甚至愤怒, 智慧之道:守护你的心 我们如何帮助年轻人避免这条道路? 詹姆斯给青少年一些实际的鼓励,让他们在一夜之间在卧室以外的地方充电电话.
他还提供了一份自查问题清单,帮助他们提高自我意识,他呼吁遵守家庭规则,例如只在家庭的空地使用装置。 但最终,詹姆斯相信,使用良好的技术不仅仅涉及遵循一个做和不做的清单。
他写道, 我们不需要一连串的规则, 每次苹果公司发布新手机或新社交媒体应用时, 我们需要智慧。 (16-17) 普罗活佛说:"对耶和华的恐惧是智慧的开始,对圣者的知识是洞察力"(9:10).
詹姆斯明白,智慧和上帝的知识的不断增长,不仅需要调整一个人的屏幕时间设置,还需要守护一个人的心。 詹姆斯鼓励青少年将心想成一个国王或女王所居住的宫殿. 他说,“在任何皇家宫殿里,你肯定能找到士兵来监视谁和什么人可以接触到里面非常重要的国王或女王”;
他认为,这些警卫是我们的习惯,“士兵的力量决定了宫殿的保护程度”(158)。 在书的早期,詹姆斯召集少年来学习辨识.
当他解开这种习惯时,他警告他们不要听那些质疑父母权威的社交媒体影响者所唱的警笛:“当一个不了解你或关心你的网络影响者以一种方式谈论你的父母或导师,使你更希望信任这些人,而影响者更多,这是你所听到的都是虚假的大规模迹象”(44)。
但詹姆斯并不只是告诉年轻人逃离数字技术的危险;他还诱使他们树立习惯,帮助他们培养美德、亲身友谊、责任感、勤奋的工作、创造力和休息。 对于父母来说,这些习惯中有许多是相互关联的。
例如,在介绍中,詹姆斯鼓励青少年与家长,教师,牧师,或导师一起阅读他的书. 他在每个章节结尾处包括的讨论问题使该律师成为实际。 这本书也是明智的, 因为虽然《Less Scroll》,
作为父母和青年工作者,我发现詹姆斯鼓励培养一种自我认识定罪的习惯。
他呼吁读者关注网络引发愤怒、焦虑或无聊的感觉, Listless boorom是Acedia罪的一种形式:“导致你充斥无意义的事物而不能对上帝取悦的原始懒惰”(65)。 他钉住我。
我有多少次在静静的瞬间, 等待一行, 几分钟的会面, 无名无姓的无聊是阿塞迪亚罪的一种形式
但正如Brett McCracken所写 的 , “ 父母用我们自己的设备建模最终比我们对孩子说的更重要。 ” 詹姆士的书帮助我看到了自己一生中一直未能与无尽的卷轴斗争的方式。 作为父母,我们需要上帝的精神来帮助我们增强对技术习惯的自我意识。
我们需要他的恩典来帮助我们 向那些我们父母和领导的孩子承认这些失败 我们需要一个智慧的心脏 和电话袋的故意, 不仅在青年小组会议上,而且我们一生。 Scroll Less, Live More帮助青少年和家长发展他们所需要的技术技能,以过着根植于现实并充满智慧的生活.
author: Jared Kennedy

title: Effective Altruists and the Spreadsheet Gospel
summary: Effective altruism commands us to love our neighbor yet dissolves that neighbor into a statistic. It asks for the fruit of the image of God while denying the root.
summary_zh: 在过去十年中,一种新兴的世俗哲学在硅谷生根. 它现在推动了许多关于政治和技术的对话,特别是它的思想决定了我们社会如何对待人工智能。 这种世界观被称作“有效的利他主义”,它正在有一个时刻。 经济学人最近称这个哲学是“本世纪最大的思想 ” , 并称这个运动为“可喜但危险的 ” 。
title_zh: 有效的利他主义者和电子表格福音
content: Over the past decade, an emergent secular philosophy has taken root in Silicon Valley. It now drives many conversations around politics and technology, particularly as its ideas shape how our society approaches artificial intelligence. Known as “effective altruism,” this worldview is having a moment. The Economist recently called the philosophy “this century’s biggest idea” and labeled the movement as “admirable, but dangerous.” Even as this philosophy is moving markets and shaping global debates, many Christians are unfamiliar with it. As a Christian and tech-policy analyst based in Washington, DC, where many of these conversations are taking place, I want to explain what effective altruism is, examine what it promises and where it fails to deliver, and show why this budding movement is incongruent with and a poor substitute for the gospel. What Is Effective Altruism? Effective altruism emerged in the late 2000s and early 2010s from the convergence of several intellectual movements, particularly utilitarian philosophy and evidence-based philanthropy. Australian academic Peter Singer provided an important foundation with his 1972 essay “ Famine, Affluence and Morality ,” where he argues that people have a moral obligation to prevent suffering when they can do so at relatively little cost to themselves. At its core, effective altruism is consequentialist, judging the rightness of an action chiefly by its outcomes. The tenets of effective altruism are straightforward: People should use reason, logic, and personal resources to maximize the good they do in society. The Centre for Effective Altruism explains , “We’re committed to prioritizing actions that benefit more lives over actions that benefit a few—that saving a billion lives is more important than saving ten.” The tenets of effective altruism are straightforward: People should use reason, logic, and personal resources to maximize the good they do in society. The movement took shape with the founding of several philanthropic organizations, such as GiveWell and 80,000 Hours . These groups emphasize measuring charitable impact, directing money toward the most effective actions, and choosing “high-impact” careers based on their potential to do good. Their approach to charitable giving has produced endeavors to improve global health , animal welfare , and economic disparities , among other areas. Over the past decade, effective altruism has expanded its scope, focusing on posterity and “longtermism,” the belief that “positively influencing the longterm future is a key moral priority of our time.” The Economist notes a belief this leads to: “Those not born yet should be weighed in the balance—and there could be trillions of them. Many EAs are ‘longtermists’ who feel bound to forestall risks in the distant future, even if that starves today’s good causes, such as helping the desperately poor.” This belief manifests itself in a focus on concerns such as existential risk (e.g., climate change or the next pandemic), nuclear proliferation, and artificial intelligence. For many in Silicon Valley, advanced AI is the defining problem of our day. The concern about a potential AI apocalypse explains why the movement has invested heavily in AI research, AI companies, and AI advocacy and safety. It’s not difficult to see why this philosophy has a natural audience among AI researchers and Silicon Valley tech luminaries. Effective altruism enables technologists to approach ethics in a way that can feel familiar: a series of probabilities, tradeoffs, and expected results—measuring an individual’s moral standing as mathematic calculations, similar to the process of building a software program where different inputs result in varied outputs. For ambitious individuals accustomed to solving complicated projects through ingenuity and critical analysis, this movement delivers reassuring community in an industry that often feels isolating. Adherents have a sense of higher purpose and calling as they’re suddenly confronted with extraordinary individual wealth and wrestle with the consequences of their technological discoveries. It’s hard to describe effective altruism without addressing its more eccentric views, some of which divide the movement itself. For example, the focus on animal welfare has led many in the movement to believe that any and all sentient beings share the same moral value, including but not limited to shrimp . Yes, since a dollar can go a long way to protect the well-being of a single crustacean , this cause could be the most efficient use of charitable giving. Notably, the effective altruist community has also drawn scrutiny for its sexual culture. A 2023 Time investigation highlighted how the movement’s overwhelmingly male membership, heavy overlap between work and home life, and its subculture of polyamory (which some have promoted as more rational than monogamy) has created a “culture of sexual harassment and abuse.” These dynamics have caused many—including Christians—to be concerned about the group’s outsize influence on culture. What Effective Altruism Promises (and Fails to Deliver) Effective altruism’s turn toward longtermism promises that the right people, armed with the right understanding of the stakes, can steer humanity safely through an uncertain future. Many in this community believe their adherence to consequentialism and longtermism gives them a special moral qualification to shape public policy. In their own eyes, effective altruists are the men and women of the hour. This conviction has moved from theory into practice. Political engagement by adherents has increased both on the public stage and backstage through building and funding civil society institutions to influence policymakers to embrace their ideology. One of the movement’s most prominent figures (though he has denied belonging to it), Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, has been leaning on this philosophy to guide his leadership of his company and shape his approach to the future of AI . Yet for all its ambition, the movement struggles to deliver on what it promises. Effective altruism’s confidence in its own reasoning to navigate the future is a hubristic claim to possess unprecedented human knowledge. Any ethic that judges right and wrong by outcomes assumes we can reliably know what our actions will produce. It treats the future as a closed system of causes and effects that the right person or algorithm can calculate. But human knowledge is finite. We can’t trace the full effects of a single choice, much less forecast the welfare of billions of potential lives. At best, an outcome-based ethic can render its moral verdict only in hindsight. Most fundamentally, effective altruism fails us because it’s an ethic without a moral foundation. It has a laudable premise: Too many people around the globe are suffering, and those with means should help. Adherents can accurately quantify certain societal woes and calculate which actions could most efficiently produce the greatest benefit. But the philosophy largely assumes the moral obligations on which those calculations depend. In Singer’s foundational essay, he uses an illustration of a man wearing expensive sneakers who walks past a drowning child. He does a moral calculation that it’s better to save the child even if it ruins his shoes. The illustration works only because we already know the child matters and that walking past would be monstrous. But a strictly consequentialist framework can’t tell us why . If people are ultimately containers of welfare to be added up, then no one has worth in himself. Each matters only as a quantity in a calculation. And who decides which quantities count? Without an external source of moral truth, the answer is ultimately the individual. Each effective altruist must reason his way to his own conclusion about what “the most good” is, and no authority outside himself can tell him he’s wrong. Taken to its logical end, this leaves room for almost anything
content_zh:
在过去十年中,一种新兴的世俗哲学在硅谷生根. 它现在推动了许多关于政治和技术的对话,特别是它的思想决定了我们社会如何对待人工智能。 这种世界观被称作“有效的利他主义”,它正在有一个时刻。
经济学人最近称这个哲学是“本世纪最大的思想 ” , 并称这个运动为“可喜但危险的 ” 。 即使这种哲学正在推动市场和形成全球辩论,许多基督徒对它并不熟悉。
作为总部设在华盛顿特区的基督教和技术政策分析者,我想解释一下这些对话是何等有效的利他主义,审视它所承诺的以及它未能兑现之处,并表明为什么这个萌芽的运动与福音不相干,并且是一个糟糕的代名词。 什么是有效的替代主义?
2000年代后期和2010年代初,有效的利他主义从几个知识运动,特别是功利主义哲学和以证据为基础的慈善活动趋同而出.
澳大利亚学者彼得·辛格以他1972年的论文"饥荒,富裕和道德"为重要基础,他在该作中认为,当人们能够以相对较少的代价来预防痛苦时,他们有道德义务. 有效的利他主义的核心是结果主义,主要根据其结果判断行动是否正确。
有效的利他主义原则是直截了当的:人们应该利用理性、逻辑和个人资源来最大限度地发挥其在社会中的效益。
“有效替代主义中心”解释说,“我们致力于优先考虑有利于更多生命的行动,而不是有利于少数人的行动——拯救十亿生命比拯救十亿生命更重要。 ” 有效的利他主义原则是直截了当的:人们应该利用理性、逻辑和个人资源来最大限度地发挥其在社会中的效益。
随着几个慈善组织的成立, 这些团体强调衡量慈善影响,将资金用于最有效的行动,并根据他们做好事的潜力选择“高影响”职业。
他们的慈善捐赠方法 带来了改善全球卫生、动物福利和经济差距的努力。
在过去的十年中,有效的利他主义扩大了它的范围,把重点放在后人和“长期主义”上,认为“积极影响长期的未来是我们时代的主要道德优先事项”。 《经济学家》指出,这导致了一种信念:“那些尚未出生的,应该加以权衡,而且可能有上万亿美元。
许多职业介绍所是“长期主义者 ” , 他们认为他们有义务在遥远的将来预防风险, 即使这饿死今天的好原因, 这种信念表现在关注存在风险(如气候变化或下个大流行病)、核扩散和人工智能等关注。
对硅谷的许多人来说,先进的AI是我们当今的决定性问题. 对AI可能启示录的担忧解释了为什么该运动在AI研究、AI公司以及AI的倡导和安全方面投入了大量资金. 为何这个哲学在AI研究人员和硅谷科技流派中有自然的读者,
有效的利他主义使技术专家能够以能够感到熟悉的方式处理伦理问题:一系列概率、取舍和预期结果 -- -- 衡量个人的道德地位作为数学计算,类似于建立一个软件程序的过程,不同投入导致不同的产出。
对于习惯于通过智慧和批判性分析解决复杂项目的野心勃勃的个人来说,这一运动在一个常常感到孤立的行业中为社区带来安慰。 坚持者有更高的目的感, 并召唤他们突然面对着非凡的个人财富,
很难描述有效的利他主义, 例如,由于注重动物福利,运动中许多人认为,任何和所有神灵生物都具有同样的道德价值,包括但不限于虾类。
是的,因为一美元对保护单一甲壳类动物的福祉有很长的路要走,因此这一事业可能是慈善捐赠的最有效用途。 值得注意的是,有效的利他主义社区也对其性文化进行了审查。
2023年时间调查凸显了该运动绝大多数男性成员、工作与家庭生活严重重叠、以及其多元文化(有些人提倡这种文化比一夫一妻制更合理)如何创造了“性骚扰和性虐待文化 ” 。 这些动态导致包括基督教徒在内的许多人担心该团体对文化的影响过大。
有效的利他主义向长期主义的转变会保证,以正确理解利害关系为武装的正确人民能够安全地引导人类度过一个不确定的未来。 这个社区的许多人认为,他们坚持后果主义和长期主义,使他们具有制定公共政策的特殊道德资格。
在他们自己的眼中,有效的利他主义者是时空的男女. 这种信念已经从理论转变为实践。 通过建立和资助民间社会机构来影响决策者接受其意识形态,信徒在公共舞台和后台的政治参与都有所增加。
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei(虽然他否认属于这个运动)最有名的人物之一, 然而,运动的雄心壮志却在努力兑现它的承诺。
有效的利他主义相信它自己为未来航行的推理,是一种傲慢地宣称拥有前所未有的人类知识。 通过结果判断对错的任何伦理都假定我们能够可靠地知道我们的行动将产生什么。 它把未来视为一个封闭的由正确人或算法可以计算的因果关系系统. 但人类的知识是有限的。
我们无法追踪单一选择的全部效果,更无法预测数十亿潜在生命的福祉。 充其量,基于结果的伦理只有在事后才能作出道德判断。 最根本的,有效的利他主义使我们失望,因为它是一个没有道德基础的伦理。
它有一个值得称赞的前提:全球有太多的人在受苦受难,那些有财力的人应当提供帮助。 坚持者可以准确地量化某些社会灾难,并计算哪些行动能够最有效地产生最大效益。 但哲学基本上承担了这些计算所依赖的道德义务。
在Singer的基礎作文中,他用一幅插图,说明一个穿昂贵运动鞋的人走过一个被淹死的孩子. 他做了一个道德的计算, 认为救孩子更好, 这个插图之所以有效,只是因为我们已经知道儿童的重要性,而且走过去将是可怕的。 但严格地说,
如果人们最终是福利的容器 来加起来, 那么没有人有价值自己。 每种物质在计算中仅作为数量。 谁决定多少数量? 没有道德真理的外部来源,答案最终是个人.
每个有效的利他论者必须解释他自己对什么是“最美好的”的结论, 任何外部权威都不能告诉他自己错了。 顺理成章地说,这为几乎一切留下了空间

content: The older I get, the more convinced I am that a posture of gratitude is key to a life of joy. God’s gifts are constant and abundant—his daily provision of life and breath far more than we deserve. Being alert to the constancy of his gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention . That’s why Thanksgiving is such a great holiday. It’s at least one day dedicated to pausing and taking stock, giving our attention to the Giver of all good gifts. Being alert to the constancy of God’s gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention. But it’s a shame Thanksgiving is just one day. Because really, we should practice gratitude constantly. What if, as a start, we dedicated the whole month of November to giving thanks? What if we dedicated time each day this month to intentionally naming God’s provision and giving him thanks? To help, I created a new playlist all about giving thanks to God. title: The Voice of the Martyrs: Prayers of the Persecuted
summary: We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners.
summary_zh: " 耶和华说,多久? . . .
title_zh: 殉道者的声音：受迫害者的祈祷
content: “How long, O LORD? . . . Pour out your anger. . . . Let the avenging of the outpoured blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes!” (Ps. 79:5–6, 10). As you’re reading through Psalms and you stumble across Psalm 79, you can’t help but wonder what to do with this very Old Testament-sounding prayer. Surely, Asaph needed to be educated in the gospel, right? Revelation 6:9–10 describes the martyrs in heaven who have been slain for their testimony to the gospel and places Psalm 79 on their lips: “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” Scholars agree the prayer of Psalm 79 is the likely background for the prayer of the martyrs, furthering our appreciation of this as a prayer for the church. It’s a prayer of and for the persecuted church. As we stand alongside them, we have divine warrant to pray Psalm 79 on their behalf. Trevor Laurence explains , “The vengeance petition of Rev. 6:9–10 thus supplies a model for the ongoing prayer of Christ’s body on earth.” Rather than being contrary to New Testament ethics, then, Psalm 79 fuels the church’s longing for every wrong to be made right. Nevertheless, you may still wonder, How do I take up a psalm like this in prayer for my persecuted brothers and sisters without falling into vindictive rage and vengefulness? Thankfully, Psalm 79 provides the guidelines needed to answer this question. Pray in Response to Horrific Injustice Verses 1–4 catalog the horrors God’s people suffered at the hands of the Babylonians who destroyed their temple: They defiled God’s holy place, they gave the flesh of God’s faithful ones to the beasts of the earth, they poured out their blood like water and refused them a proper burial, and they were the cause of God’s people becoming a taunt to their neighbors. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. This has two implications. First, these prayers do not give license for us to pray such things against just anyone. Second, if we object to such prayers, they challenge us to ask whether we have ever faced anything close to the agonizing evil that gave birth to this prayer. As Jamie Grant posits , “Perhaps our reluctance to appropriate the psalms of enmity is rooted in the comfort of our lives.” If we knew the kind of horror Psalm 79 speaks of (and that our persecuted brothers and sisters endure daily), perhaps we wouldn’t be so quick to dismiss these psalms. Pray for the Glory of God As psalms like this respond to such evil, they are fundamentally concerned with God’s glory. We see this in Psalm 79:6, where the nations’ refusal to call on God’s name is the motive behind Asaph’s cry. Likewise, verse 9 cites the glory of God’s name and his “name’s sake” as a rationale for God to answer this request. And verse 10 is concerned that, at present, the onlooking nations say, “Where is their God?” So Asaph asks that God’s justice would be made known among the nations (v. 10), and that God’s people might praise him for it (v. 13). The glory of God is the ultimate end of the imprecatory psalms. Or as James Hamilton says , “The glory of God in salvation through judgment is the center of the theology of Psalms.” The same is true of imprecatory psalms like Psalm 79. Their controlling desire is “Hallowed be thy name.” Pray with a Humble Posture The imprecatory psalms are not prayed in a spirit of self-righteousness; those praying them understand their need for God’s grace. They pray for justice from a posture of humility, where they confess that this judgment is what they too deserve apart from God’s grace (vv. 8–9). This is not unlike the widow’s prayer for justice in Luke 18:1–8 being paired with the parable of the Pharisee and tax collector in verses 9–14. We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners. We pray the second petition of the Lord’s Prayer (“Thy kingdom come”) with the fifth petition also in mind (“Forgive us our debts”). Pray with a Desire for Repentance If God could turn his anger away from repentant sinners in exile (Ps. 79:5), then he could do the same for Israel’s enemies. While this is not explicit in Psalm 79, its near neighbor Psalm 83, at the conclusion of this section of Asaph psalms, prays that God would fill the faces of these enemy nations with shame “that they might seek [the LORD’s name]” (v. 16). It is legitimate to see this desire as qualifying the earlier imprecations in the Asaph collection (indeed, in the whole Psalter). Hamilton even suggests every prayer for judgment in the psalms should be read as if containing an implicit “footnote” desiring repentance as a possibility. Pray with the Hope of Final Justice The prayers of judgment, like Psalm 79, are not petty prayers incompatible with a Christian ethic. God’s people pray in response to horrific injustice, aimed at the glory of God, with a posture of humility and openness to their enemies becoming God’s friends. We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners. The imprecatory psalms, then, fit perfectly with the gospel of Jesus Christ. And they arm the church to intercede for the saints in a day when our Christian brothers and sisters suffer great harm throughout the world. We long for God to answer these prayers through the conversion of our enemies. But if they remain impenitent, it is only right for God to bring justice. And it is thus right for us to pray that he would.

author: Ryan Swale

title: Martin Luther in 5 Latin Phrases
summary: Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift.
summary_zh: 马丁·路德于1483年11月10日生于德国艾斯莱本. 第二天他在圣彼得和保罗教堂被洗礼. 7岁时,路德进入了曼斯菲尔德拉丁学校. 他在那里学习了拉丁语的语法和祷告,并记住了艾索普的"寓言".
title_zh: 马丁·路德的5个拉丁短语
content: Martin Luther was born in Eisleben, Germany, on November 10, 1483. He was christened at Saints Peter and Paul Church the next day. At age 7, Luther entered the Mansfeld Latin School. There he learned Latin grammar and prayers, and he memorized Aesop’s Fables . From those early years through his time studying at boarding school in Magdeburg then later at the University of Erfurt, Luther was a diligent student. He kept up with his Latin, and several important Latin phrases appear throughout Luther’s writings. Five of them serve as a good summary of his life and chief theological emphases. 1. Iustitia Dei In July 1505, Luther was caught in a fierce thunderstorm. Panicked and terrified, he bargained with God, promising to become a monk. After entering the monastery, Luther was again overcome by fear. When he led his first mass as a priest, it wasn’t an occasion of joy. Instead, it was filled with trembling. As the service began, Luther took his place at the front of the chapel, and he began to recite the Latin prayers. Luther knew that God is perfect in judgment and completely without sin. So as he thought about iustitia Dei , “the righteousness of God” (Rom. 1:17), terror struck him. Biographer Roland H. Bainton describes the thoughts that plagued Luther’s mind: Who am I that I should . . . raise my hands to the divine Majesty? The angels surround him. At his nod the earth trembles . . . [but] I am dust and ashes. When Luther held up the bread and wine, he shook so badly he almost dropped the cup. During those years growing up in school and at the monastery, Luther only thought of God’s righteousness, or justice, as his active judgment against human sin. He later wrote , Though I lived as a monk without reproach, I felt and knew I was a sinner before God. I had an extremely disturbed conscience. . . . I hated the righteous God who punishes sinners. 2. Extra nos In 1512, Luther became a university professor in Wittenberg. As he studied the Bible for his lectures, he began to see God’s righteousness in a new light. Luther saw how Jesus Christ took on our humanity, how he lived a perfect life and died the painful and shameful death of the cross to take the punishment due for sin. He saw how God raised Jesus from the dead, and how he now justifies Christians by faith. God declares that in his sight, Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift of salvation. Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift. What happened when Luther made this discovery? Here’s how he described it: “I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates.” After that day, Luther began to teach that God gives Christians his “alien righteousness,” that is, a righteousness that comes extra nos , “from outside of us.” Our righteousness isn’t from us; it doesn’t come from what we do. It can’t be earned by saying a prayer or even by having a good attitude. Our righteousness is ultimately found in and belongs to another, our Savior Jesus Christ. 3. Crux sola est nostra theologia On October 31, 1517, Luther famously posted his Ninety-five Theses on the door of Castle Church. In it, Luther spoke clearly against the money-raising indulgence schemes Pope Leo X and Germany’s own Prince Albert of Brandenburg had sponsored. The next year, in April 1518, Luther defended these views at the Augustinian order’s spring meeting in Heidelberg. Luther walked to the meeting in fear. He expected the leaders there to sternly rebuke him. After all, that’s what the pope had asked them to do. But to Luther’s surprise, the leaders at the meeting welcomed his defense with excitement. What did Luther say that got his new friends so excited? In his Heidelberg Disputation , Luther described two types of people—the “theologian of glory” and the “theologian of the cross.” Theologians of glory think people are capable and smart enough to know God through human reason. They also say we can know who God’s righteous people are because we see God reward them with political power, success, and wealth. Though Luther didn’t use Albert’s and Leo’s names in his disputation, it’s clear he was talking about their greedy doctrine of indulgences when he described the theologian of glory. Luther’s “theologian of the cross,” by contrast, knows it’s not always people who appear good, beautiful, and powerful by worldly standards who truly know God. After all, Jesus didn’t look glorious on the cross. “One deserves to be called a true theologian,” Luther wrote , “who sees God even in suffering.” As Paul wrote, “God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong” (1 Cor. 1:27). After Heidelberg, the phrase “ Crux sola est nostra theologia ” (“The cross alone is our theology”) became a rallying cry for Luther’s followers. It still is today. 4. Oratio, meditatio, tentatio Luther’s teaching set the Protestant Reformation in motion. In support of his reforms, Luther published hundreds of books, sermons, and hymns. Significantly, he also translated the entire Bible into the language of Germany’s common people. But Luther didn’t want common people to merely read Scripture. He wanted them to study it too. In the 1539 preface to the Wittenberg edition of his German writings, Luther wrote, “God himself lives in the Bible. Therefore, worthy Christian: get in, get in!” Luther gave his readers three rules for digging into God’s Word. Each has its own Latin term: prayer ( oratio ), meditation ( meditatio ), and suffering ( tentatio ). A ‘theologian of the cross’ knows it’s not always people who appear good, beautiful, and powerful by worldly standards who truly know God. The first rule is kept before we read the Bible. Luther wrote, “Kneel down in your private room and with humility, pray to God to give you his Holy Spirit to enlighten and guide and give you understanding.” The second rule is kept while reading: “Read and reread the very words written down in the Bible. Observe and think about what the Holy Spirit means.” The last rule is kept when we practice what the Scriptures say. Luther said, As soon as you begin to know God’s word, the devil will afflict you. . . . This suffering will teach you how right, true, sweet, lovely, mighty, and comforting God’s word is. It is wisdom supreme. 5. Simul iustus et peccator Luther was zealous and driven. He once said, “When I want to compose, write, pray, and preach well, I must be angry.” But while anger may have given Luther energy for work, it too often burned out of control. Sadly, today, Luther is as famous for his harsh words spoken against his enemies and the Jews as he is for recovering the biblical doctrine of justification. Throughout his life, Luther taught that believers are simul iustus et peccator . That’s Latin for “simultaneously justified and a sinner.” Both realities are true of every Christian. Both were true of Luther. He was a broken man who desperately needed God’s grace, and he knew it. Luther died while visiting Eisleben on February 18, 1546. Before he died, Luther scribbled out his last written words: “We are beggars. This is true.” Luther knew he could never earn God’s grace. Salvation isn’t won through indulgences or daily prayers. This is what Luther had discovered from the Bible and taught again to the world. God sent his only Son. Christ has overcome the world. All he asks of poor, begging sinners is that we believe.
content_zh:
马丁·路德于1483年11月10日生于德国艾斯莱本. 第二天他在圣彼得和保罗教堂被洗礼. 7岁时,路德进入了曼斯菲尔德拉丁学校. 他在那里学习了拉丁语的语法和祷告,并记住了艾索普的"寓言".
从早年到后来在马格德堡的寄宿学校学习,路德是一名勤奋的学生。 他跟上了拉丁语,几个重要的拉丁语短语也出现在路德的著作中. 其中5个是他的生平和首席神学重心的良好总结. 1. 联合国
1505年7月,路德被猛烈的雷暴所困. 惊慌惊恐地与上帝讨价还价,许诺成为和尚. 进入修道院后,路德再次被恐惧所克服. 当他第一次作为牧师主持弥撒时, 相反,充满了颤抖。
随着礼拜的开始,路德在礼拜堂前取而代之,他开始背诵拉丁语祈祷. 路德知道上帝在判断上是完美的,并且完全没有罪恶. 因此,当他想到了iustitia Dei“上帝的公义”(1:17)时,恐怖袭击了他。 传记作者罗兰·H·班顿(Roland H. Bainton)描述了困扰路德思想的思想:我应该是谁?
举起手来见圣上? 众天神围绕他. 在他点头的时候,大地会颤抖... ...但是,我是灰尘和灰烬。 当路德拿起面包和葡萄酒时,他摇得这么厉害,差点把杯子掉下. 在那些年里,路德在学校和修道院里长大,他只把上帝的正义或正义视为他对人类罪恶的积极判断。
他后来写道, 虽然我作为一个和尚生活 没有责备, 我感觉和知道我是上帝面前的罪人。 我有一个极度不安的良心。 我憎恨惩罚罪人的善良之神 2. 1512年,路德成为维滕贝格的大学教授. 当他为他的演讲而学习圣经时,他开始在新的光芒下看到上帝的正义.
路德看到耶稣基督如何对待我们的人性,他如何过上完美的生活并死于十字架上的痛苦而可耻的死亡来取取罪的惩罚. 他看见了上帝如何使耶稣从死地复活,以及他现在如何通过信仰为基督徒辩护. 上帝宣布,在他看来,耶稣的完美生活和牺牲的死亡对所有信徒都很重要。
因此上帝的正义不仅仅是他的判断。 这也是他的救赎天赋。 耶稣的完美生活和牺牲的死亡是所有信徒的计数. 因此上帝的正义不仅仅是他的判断。 这也是他的天赋。 当路德做出这个发现时发生了什么?
他是这样描述的 : “ 我感到我再次出生,并通过开放的大门进入了天堂。 ” 在那一天之后,路德开始教导上帝给予基督徒“外星人的正义 ” , 即“来自我们以外的”一种格外不义的正义。 我们的正义不是来自我们,
祈祷, 我们的正义最终被发现 并属于另一个,我们的救主耶稣基督。 3. Crux sola est nostra Godologia 1517年10月31日,路德将他的"95个本事"出名地贴在了城堡教堂的门上.
路德在书中明确表示反对教皇利奥十世和德国自己的勃兰登堡阿尔贝特亲王赞助的集资宽恕计划。 次年,即1518年4月,路德在海德堡举行的奥古斯丁会令春季会议上为这些观点辩护. 路德在恐惧中走去开会. 他期望那里的领导人严厉斥责他。
这毕竟是教皇要求他们做的。 但令路德惊讶的是,与会领导人激动地欢迎他的辩护. 路德怎么说 他的新朋友这么兴奋?
路德在他的"海德堡争论"中描述了两类人——"荣耀之神"和"十字架之神". 荣耀的神学家们认为,人的能力和智慧足以通过人类理性来认识上帝. 他们也说,我们可以知道上帝的善良人民是谁,因为我们看到真主以政治力量、成功和财富奖励他们。
虽然路德在争论中并没有使用阿尔伯特和利奥的名字,但很明显,当他描述荣耀的神学家时,他在谈论他们贪婪的宽恕理论。 相对而言,路德的“十字架神学家”知道,并非总能让世界标准显示良好、美丽和强大的人真正了解上帝。 毕竟耶稣在十字架上并不光荣。
路德写道 : “ 一个人应该被称为真正的神学家,” 路德写道,“谁在痛苦中看到上帝。 ” 正如保罗所写道的:“上帝选择了世界上的愚蠢来羞辱智者;上帝选择了世界上的弱者来羞辱强者。” 海德堡之后, " Crux sola est nostra Godologia " ( " 十字架是我们的神学 " )成为路德信徒的呼声。
今天还是这样。 4. Oratio、meditatio、tentatio Luther的教义使新教改革运动开始。 为支持他的改革,路德出版了上百本书,布道,并作"赞". 重要的是,他还将整个"圣经"翻译成了德国普通人的语言. 但路德并不想普通人只读圣经。 他希望他们也研究它。
路德在他的德文著作"维滕贝格"1539年版的前言中写道:"上帝自己活在圣经中. 因此,值得的基督徒:上车,上车!” 路德给了读者三条钻入上帝之道的规则. 每个词都有自己的拉丁名词:祷告(oratio),冥想(meditatio)和苦难(tentatio).
一个“十字架的神学家”知道,并非总有人以世界标准看起来是好人、美丽人和强大的人真正了解上帝。 第一条规则在我们读出"圣经"之前被保留.
路德写道:“跪在你的私人房间里谦逊地祈祷真主赐予你他的圣灵以启蒙、引导和谅解。” 第二条规则在读取时保留:“读取并重读圣经所写的文字。 观察并思考圣灵的意义。” 最后一个规则是当我们实践圣经所说的话时,
路德说,一旦你明白上帝的话,恶魔就会折磨你。 这种痛苦将教你如何正确、真实、甜蜜、可爱、强大并安慰上帝的话。 这是智慧至上。 5. Simul iustus et peccator Luther是狂热和有动力的。
他曾经说过:“当我想写作、写作、祈祷和讲道的时候,我一定生气了。” 但是,虽然愤怒可能已经让路德精力充沛地工作,但是它经常被烧得失控. 可悲的是,今天,路德以其对敌人和犹太人的严酷言辞而出名,如同他收复了圣经中的辩解学说而出名.
路德一生教导信徒们, 这在拉丁语中是“极端合理和有罪者 ” 。 每个基督教徒都一样 路德也一样 他是一个破碎的人,他迫切需要上帝的恩惠,他知道这一点。 1546年2月18日路德在访问艾斯莱本时去世.
在他死前,路德写出他最后的文字:“我们是乞丐。 这是事实。” Luther知道他永远得不到上帝的恩惠。 救赎不是通过宽容或日常祈祷而赢得的。 这是路德从圣经中发现的,并再次向世界传授. 上帝派他唯一的儿子 基督战胜了这个世界 他只要求贫穷 乞求罪人 我们相信
author: Jared Kennedy

summary: Marriages with one or both spouses employed in ministry face unique pressures, challenges, and opportunities.

content: Marriages with one or both spouses employed in ministry face unique pressures, challenges, and opportunities. title: ‘Mosquito Bowl’: Football Stars on the Front Lines
summary: Peter Berg’s ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ is essentially ‘Friday Night Lights’ meets ‘Hacksaw Ridge.’
summary_zh: Peter Berg's The Mosquito Bowl本质上是周五夜光会合哈克锯脊。 这是一部与"周五夜光"(Gritty handhip camera, muted color paget, Sky后摇滚乐中的爆炸)相同的创意氛围的电影, 也与伯格的"星期五夜光"(The Mosquito Bowl (现在在剧院出演; 11月25日来到Netflix))一样,
title_zh: “蚊子碗” ：前线的足球明星
content: Peter Berg’s The Mosquito Bowl is essentially Friday Night Lights meets Hacksaw Ridge . It’s a movie with the same creative vibe as Friday Night Lights (gritty handheld camera, muted color palette, Explosions in the Sky post-rock soundtrack) but applied to a brutally violent true story of WWII’s Battle of Okinawa, one of the single bloodiest battles of the 20th century. Also like Berg’s Friday Night Lights , The Mosquito Bowl ( out now in theaters ; coming to Netflix November 25) is based on a book by Pulitzer Prize–winning journalist Buzz Bissinger . The 2022 book—subtitled A Game of Life and Death in World War II —only has one chapter (of 41) devoted to the actual 1944 football game dubbed “The Mosquito Bowl.” Most of the book is about the war, and the young men who left wives, kids, and promising NFL careers to fight it. Likewise, Berg’s film adaptation is mostly a somber, unflinching WWII film, with a brief reprieve of joy in the form of a football game on Guadalcanal between the 4th and 29th regiments of the 6th Marine Division. Just as in Friday Night Lights , where the drama of high school football parallels the struggles and triumphs of life off the field, the football game in The Mosquito Bowl parallels the “game of life and death” that surrounds the men at war. Sports are interesting in this way: They provide escape from real life but also training for it, an arena of danger and high stakes but not ultimate stakes. Sports often map onto life—we draw up plans and plays but have to improvise; we get hurt but can heal; we thrive individually through teamwork; sometimes we win and sometimes we lose. Yet sports are unlike real life too. Winning or losing on the field is a matter of trophies and glory, but off the field, it can be a matter of life and death. Young Men Willing to Fight and Die The Mosquito Bowl (rated R for graphic war violence and language), opens with a well-known epigraph from Herbert Hoover : Older men declare war. But it is youth that must fight and die. And it is youth who must inherit the tribulation, the sorrow, and the triumphs that are the aftermath of war. This is a movie about youth—or rather, the passage from youth into adulthood that war accelerates. This is a movie about youth—or rather, the passage from youth into adulthood that war accelerates. The movie opens with muddy college football scenes in the fall of 1941, as the four central characters are introduced: John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Brown quarterback; Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård), University of Wisconsin tackle; Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson), Purdue fullback; and Dave Schreiner (Tom Francis), Wisconsin end. They were all-star athletes with promising futures. Many of them were collegiate All-Americans and drafted by NFL teams. Yet December 7, 1941, happened, and their futures were all changed. Once bound together by football skill, friendly rivalry, and fierce competition on the gridiron, these men soon bonded in a different setting: as marines in WWII’s savage Pacific theater. Instead of fighting for yards on the field, they fought for ground in a war of attrition on Okinawa. Instead of a football in hand, they carried guns and bayonets. Instead of tackling their opponents, they wrestled them to the death in hand-to-hand combat. Like many in the Greatest Generation, these men volunteered to enlist and fight. The Mosquito Bowl celebrates their duty and sacrifice. In one scene, Baumann’s younger brother says, “You don’t have to go,” to which Baumann replies, “I do. I’m needed.” It’s hard to imagine star athletes, whether collegiate or professional, volunteering to go to war in 2026. But in 1943, it was normal. Okinawa, Bissinger writes in the book, was “by far the largest collection of athletes ever to die in a single battle.” And in the entirety of WWII, 21 NFL players died in combat, as well as two players from Major League Baseball. Why were they so willing to lay down their lives? Perhaps back then, men had the bigger horizon more in view. Life isn’t about serving oneself. It’s about serving others, fighting for things bigger than personal fulfillment. As Dave Schreiner tells John McLaughry, “This is us sacrificing for the unborn. What other real thing is there? What’s the point in all of this if it’s not for passing something on?” Numbed by War-Movie Violence The Mosquito Bowl honors the Greatest Generation and is commendable in its straightforward embrace of manly virtues like duty and sacrifice. But I disliked several aspects of the film. One is the language. I realize wartime soldiers in every era tend to be prolific in their employment of profane language. But even if men in the 1940s were as creative with the f-word as they are in this movie, is it really essential to the movie? It makes the film much less likely to be watched by families, which is a shame because it’s the sort of thing dads might want to watch with their younger sons. I also wish Berg had given less screen time to bloody battles and more time to quieter character moments and the titular football game. I get that it’s important to underscore the savage bloodbath that was the Pacific theater, and I get that the joyful escape of football is most pronounced when juxtaposed with the horrific realities of war. But it’s hard for contemporary war movies to viscerally depict the “war is hell” experience after the genre has been so saturated. Edward Berger’s adaptation of All Quiet on the Western Front (2022) felt like the final word on war-movie blood and guts. We’ve become numb to watching bodies get mangled every which way. Going forward, movies about savage warfare probably need to take a different approach. There are ways to capture battle horror without showing every gruesome detail. Furthermore, the desaturated, shaky-camera, chaotic choreography of war movies has become clichéd. I checked out a bit during these prolonged battle scenes. At times, it felt like Berg was inspired by Terrence Malick’s Guadalcanal movie, The Thin Red Line (one of the best war movies of all time). But what made Malick’s film so effective is that it employed violence only in a few intense, lyrical sequences, juxtaposed with long stretches of more contemplative material and tender character moments. The experience of war is important to capture accurately. But a war film becomes great when the meaning of war is also a focal point. Clint Eastwood’s WWII diptych, Flags of our Fathers and Letters from Iwo Jima (2006), strikes this balance well. The action-to-reflection ratio is not quite right in The Mosquito Bowl . Football as Far as the Curse Is Found The high point of Berg’s movie is the Mosquito Bowl game, even though it occupies too little of the overall runtime. In a movie that is rather bleak thematically and visually, the game provides a much-needed moment of joy for the characters and audience. Hosted as a morale booster for soldiers who would soon be sent to fight on Okinawa, the game (broadcast on the “mosquito radio network”) was set up to be “two-hand touch” only but quickly devolved into full-on tackle. Some of the guys wore Santa hats. There were big smiles, laughs, playful rivalry: young men allowed to be boys again. Here’s how Bissinger describes it in the prologue of his book: For roughly two hours the Mosquito Bowl wasn’t simply a reminder of what life had once been like for the players, but freedom and abandon, with the spectators captured in the same moment, screaming their heads off, whether drunk or sober. The beauty of sports, the ultimate power of it to carry you away, had never been stronger. But the scene is also bittersweet, for we know it’s not reality. Real life is harsh. Okinawa looms. Many of these boys playing football on Christmas Eve 1944 won’t live to see Christmas Eve 1945. This scene reminded me of the resonant poetry of Friday Night Lights , which depicted football in much the same way: youthful vibrancy and freewheeling joy, but tempered by the painful pressures

Peter Berg's The Mosquito Bowl本质上是周五夜光会合哈克锯脊。 这是一部与"周五夜光"(Gritty handhip camera, muted color paget, Sky后摇滚乐中的爆炸)相同的创意氛围的电影,
也与伯格的"星期五夜光"(The Mosquito Bowl (现在在剧院出演;11月25日来到Netflix))一样,
2022年的一书——被取名为"二战中生死的游戏"(A Game of Life and Death in World War)——只有一章(第41章)专门讲述了1944年被誉为"蚊子碗"的实际足球比赛. 这本书大多是关于战争的,而那些离开妻子,孩子的年轻人,以及有前途的NFL职业来对抗战争.
同样地,伯格的电影改编作品大多是一部默默无闻的WWII电影,以第6海军陆战队第4团和第29团在瓜达尔卡纳尔(Guadalcanal)上进行足球比赛的形式短暂地延缓了欢乐.
就像星期五的"夜光"一样,高中足球的戏剧与场外生活的斗争和胜利平行,"蚊子碗"(The Mosquito Bowl)的足球比赛与围攻战中男子的"生死游戏"平行. 体育是有趣的: 它们提供了逃避现实生活的机会,但也为它提供了培训,这是一个危险和利害攸关的场所,但不是最终利害攸关。
体育常常描绘在生活中——我们制定计划和玩法,但必须即兴发挥;我们受到伤害,但可以治愈;我们通过团队精神而单独地繁荣;有时我们赢,有时我们输。 然而,体育也不同于现实生活。 取胜或输于地是道道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道是道.
年轻人愿意战斗并死亡 蚊子碗(以平面战争暴力和语言评分为R),以赫伯特·胡佛出道的著名史诗":老人宣战"开场. 但是,青年必须战斗并死亡。 而正是青年必须继承三难之地,悲伤之地,而胜利之地是战争后遗症.
这是一部关于青年的电影, 这是一部关于青年的电影, 电影以泥地大学足球场景于1941年秋季开拍,因为四个中心人物被介绍:约翰·麦克劳克里(英语:John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine)),布朗四分卫;
鲍勃·鲍曼(英语:Bill Skarsgård),威斯康辛大学钓鱼台;托尼·布特克维奇(英语:Ray Nicholson),普杜克·全后卫;戴夫·施雷纳(英语:Dave Schreiner (Tom Francis)),威斯康辛大学终点. 他们是全明星运动员 前途光明 其中多为全美联队,由NFL球队起草. 然而1941年12月7日,却发生了,他们的未来都变了.
这些人一度被足球技巧、友好竞争和激烈的竞争捆绑在一起,但很快却在不同的环境下被束缚在一起:作为海军陆战队员在二战期间的野蛮太平洋剧场。 在冲绳的一次自然减员战争中,他们不是在战场上为码而战,而是为地而战. 他们没有手持足球,而是携带了枪和刺刀.
他们不但没有对付对手,反而用手相搏的方式将对手摔倒至死. 和"最伟大的一代"中的许多人一样,这些人自愿入伍并出战. 蚊子碗会庆祝他们的职责和牺牲. 在一个场景中,鲍曼的弟弟说,“你不必去,”鲍曼回答说,“我愿意。
需要我。 很难想象明星运动员, 但是在1943年,这是正常的. Bissinger在书中写道,冲绳是“迄今为止在一次战斗中死亡的运动员人数最多的集合地”。 而在整个二战中,有21名NFL球员在战斗中丧生,还有来自主力联赛棒球的两名球员.
为什么他们这么愿意牺牲自己的生命? 也许那时,男人的视野更大 生活不是为自己服务。 而是为他人服务, 正如Dave Schreiner告诉John McLaughry的那样,“这是我们为未出生的人而牺牲。 还有什么真实的?
如果不是为了传递东西, "蚊子碗"以战争电影"暴力"(War-Movie Violence The Mosquito Bowl)为荣,以直截了当地拥抱"责任"和"牺牲"等人性美德而著称. 但我不喜欢电影的几个方面。 一是语言.
我意识到每个时代的战时士兵在使用污名语言方面往往很繁多. 但是,即使20世纪40年代的男性对"f-word"的创造力和这出电影中的一样,这是否真的对电影至关重要? 这让影片不太可能被家人看,
我也希望伯格给 较少的屏幕时间 对于血腥的战斗 更多的时间 安静的角色时刻 和三角足球比赛。 我理解强调太平洋剧场的野蛮流血很重要,
但当代战争电影很难直截了当地描绘出"战争就是地狱", Edward Berger在"西部战线"(2022年)上改编的"All Quiet"(All Quiet on the Western Front (2022年)),感觉就像战争-电影"血和胆"上的最后一句话. 我们对看尸体被打乱已经麻木了。
向前看,关于野蛮战争的电影可能需要采取不同的做法。 有一些方法捕捉出战斗恐怖而不展示出每一个可怕的细节. 此外,战争电影的不饱和、摇摇欲坠、杂乱无章地编舞也成了陈词滥调。 我在这些漫长的战斗场景中检查了一下
贝格有时觉得受到特伦斯·马利克出演的瓜达尔卡纳尔电影"瘦子红线"的启发(这是有史以来最好的战争电影之一). 但马利克的影片之所以如此有效, 是因为影片只使用几起激烈的、充满诗意的相接相接的暴力事件,
